body.text: In October 2026, China’s Liaoning carrier group transited the Basilan Strait toward the Celebes Sea, at least its second reported passage since December 2025. The deployment also included a transit through the Luzon Strait. Its significance lies in demonstrating additional routes through the First Island Chain. A CSIS analysis of Japanese observations recorded Liaoning and Shandong beyond the First Island Chain for a combined 58 days in 2025, up from 32 in 2024.

For China, those options have implications beyond mere navigation. China’s expanding naval and air reach gives it more opportunities to impose costs on forces seeking to interrupt its seaborne energy supply. A blockade coalition would have to protect its own operations and its members’ trade while sustaining pressure on China.

In China’s case, the Malacca dilemma refers to its exposure to disruption of the large share of its seaborne energy imports and trade that passes through the Strait of Malacca, as well as to the coercive leverage that this vulnerability gives others. The Diplomat has already examined the strategic importance of the Strait of Malacca in previous analyses, along with and the disruptive potential of sanctions and compliance pressure. With its broader naval and air presence, however, China is making the Malacca dilemma no longer one-directional. Any blockade coalition must now account for the increased reach of the People’s Liberation Army (PLA).

One concrete way that PLA presence complicates coalition planning is surveillance. The southern Philippine approaches illustrate the burden. USNI News reported that BRP Sarangani shadowed Liaoning, while BRP Diego Silang and BRP Emilio Jacinto also monitored the group.

Yet successful local shadowing does not establish continuous coverage. Japan’s Joint Staff documented carrier flight operations on October 14 and the formation’s movement toward the South China Sea on October 15; Philippine monitoring records obtained by Bilyonaryo News Channel described tracking on October 22-23. The intervening week was not accounted for in those reports. Operational intelligence may remain undisclosed, so that gap does not establish lost contact, but the public record doesn’t support an assumption of uninterrupted Philippine surveillance.

USNI described the Philippine military’s force posture in Mindanao as focused on counter-piracy and counterinsurgency missions, while PLA Tracker’s Ben Lewis characterized the Sulu Sea as less closely watched than Luzon. Separately, Chinese ships have used the Sibutu Passage in 2019, well before the Liaoning deployment. Such activity broadens the area in which U.S. partners may need to maintain contact with Chinese forces. If Philippine coverage proves insufficient, additional U.S. or allied surveillance assets would be required, reducing what remains available for other missions.

The surveillance burden created by these southern transits matters even if the coalition does not intend to intercept ships there. A coalition need not patrol every Philippine passage to stop tankers west of Malacca. However, it would have to account for Chinese forces operating elsewhere in the theater and the additional protection required by exposed ships and support facilities. This competition for resources connects the southern transits to blockade sustainability.

Selectivity adds another burden: restricting China-bound cargo while allowing other trade requires more than identifying a vessel’s flag or next port. U.S. maritime sanctions guidance already calls for scrutiny of cargo documentation, counterparties, and ownership. Transshipment through an intermediate hub can complicate the determination of a cargo’s ultimate destination. In a blockade scenario, inspections and disputed records would consume time while Chinese military activity increases force-protection requirements. Shipowners or insurers might withdraw before an interception occurred. Such uncertainty could increase pressure on China, but it could also undermine the credibility of the U.S. promise that allied trade would remain unaffected. China’s regional presence creates leverage by making that promise harder and more expensive to keep.

The United States would face these requirements with a fleet whose sustained availability is already constrained. A 2025 Government Accountability Office review identified shortages of spare parts and qualified maintenance personnel, alongside deferred surface-ship maintenance. An August 2026 report found that maintenance delays and idle time had cost active attack submarines more than 15,000 operational days during fiscal years 2016-2025.

USS Benfold’s July 2026 engineering casualty illustrated the immediate consequences. The destroyer lost power and required towing to Subic Bay before repairs were completed. During a blockade, replacing a disabled ship’s surveillance or escort functions would draw on other assets. The problem is cumulative: more protection against Chinese interference increases demand for ships already needed for rotations, among other additional maintenance and crew-recovery demands. A coalition’s initial strength therefore says little about how much capability it can keep available month after month.

American naval constraints would increase pressure on allies to contribute, but Japan and South Korea have vulnerabilities of their own. U.S. Energy Information Administration data identify both countries as major destinations for crude oil passing through Malacca. Their governments would need assurances that participation would not jeopardize the supplies their economies require. Chinese operations across the wider region could increase the escorts and surveillance needed to protect that shipping route, further draining forces available for coalition enforcement.

The Liaoning’s operation beyond the First Island Chain does not establish an ability to threaten every tanker supplying Northeast Asia, but it illustrates the geographic breadth planners must consider when assessing possible Chinese responses. China could seek to discourage participation in any blockade by increasing the expected cost to coalition members. Allied participation therefore cannot be assumed. Japan’s Reciprocal Access Agreement with the Philippines facilitates defense cooperation, but it does not constitute advance consent to joining a blockade. Contributions to an interdiction operation would also compete with each country’s other defense requirements.

Support from the states bordering the strait is equally consequential. In April, Singaporean Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan ruled out participation in attempts to close, interdict, or impose tolls in Singapore’s neighborhood. He described Singapore, Malaysia, and Indonesia as strategically aligned in keeping the straits open, and said Singapore had conveyed its position on transit passage to both China and United States. The statement directly challenges any assumption that existing security relationships guarantee local support for maritime interdiction. Without cooperation, an enforcing coalition could face longer support routes and more demanding arrangements for access and resupply. Singapore’s position and the Philippines’ surveillance challenge are different constraints: one concerns partner alignment, the other resources and capacity. Together, they show why regional partnerships cannot be treated as ready-made reserve of enforcement capacity.
China nevertheless remains exposed beyond its immediate region. Peacetime transits do not demonstrate the ability to keep ships, aircraft, and replenishment vessels operating under attack.

A 2020 Naval War College study identified PLA logistics, air-defense, and antisubmarine limitations in the Indian Ocean. Rather than establish China’s current capability ceiling, the assessment identifies the functions that distant operations must sustain. Interdiction farther west would stretch Chinese support and protection requirements, rendering the military options demonstrated by operations around the first island chain less feasible. The regional deterrent is therefore conditional and geographically uneven, with its value lying in raising the cost of coercing China rather than eliminating China’s vulnerability to economic pressure.

Only when a coalition seeks to blockade the Malacca Strait or enforce selective interdiction against China do Chinese operations create additional force-protection requirements for coalition forces and exposed shipping. U.S. availability constraints then limit the capacity to meet those requirements, while partners’ exposure makes assurances about permitted trade harder to sustain. These interactions make coalition participation harder to justify. The Malacca dilemma, therefore, increasingly runs both ways. For the United States, the central question is whether a coalition can maintain selective interdiction long enough to meaningfully change China’s calculations while absorbing Chinese counterpressure against its own forces and its most exposed partners.
